#8277. Watch: Jessie Diggins Explains Why Sparkles Are Her Superpower

Trail Runner managing editor Abby Levene caught up with cross-country skiing superstar Jessie Diggins in Kona, Hawaii, a few days before the Ironman World Championship. In this exclusive interview, Diggins shares how she battled through a deep low to finish (and win) her first 100-miler, the lessons from cross-country skiing that she’s applying to trail running, and why she always puts on face glitter before a race.

After retiring from cross-country skiing as the most decorated American of all time, glide off into the sunset Jessie Diggins did not. The Olympic gold medalist earned one last piece of hardware in Milan-Cortina this spring—on bruised ribs no less—hung up the skis, and dove head-first into trail running.

Diggins, 35, raced the Broken Arrow Triple Crown in June, as has become her annual ritual. She then lined up against the world’s best trail runners at Sierre-Zinal in August, won the Superior 100-miler in September, and just last weekend won the (bear with me) Trail Animals Running Club Stone Cat Trail Festival 50-miler in Massachusetts.

On paper, it’s been an effortless transition into a sport Diggins swears she is just doing for fun. But of course there is so much more to the story once you dig in. I was lucky enough to catch up with Diggins at the epicenter of yet another endurance sport—the Ironman World Championship—in Kona, Hawaii, last month. She’d just come from a snorkeling expedition trying to find a sea turtle. (So far no luck.) Gazing out onto the turquoise waves crashing into shore, we chatted about what she’s learned and loved about trail running so far. That list includes (and is not limited to) how trail running really is a team sport, achieving personal goals is bigger than the results, fueling on a “washing machine” stomach is not easy, and the power of glitter translates from snowy trails to dry ones.

This interview has been edited for clarity. You can also watch some of it above.

Jessie: It was a really cool experience. It was so humbling, but so exciting to tackle a totally different challenge. I was filled with curiosity: What will this feel like? What’s going to happen to my body? What will happen inside my brain? How does this work?

Having a crew and pacers like that is very different from skiing. [In skiing] you are alone on the trail, and people can cheer for you, but you don’t actually have anyone with you on the trail. And so it was just so exciting I got to do it with a team. That was really big for me. I’m a very team-oriented person, and I would get so excited to come into the aid station and see the crew and to get to have a pacer with me. Even when I was falling apart and couldn’t even  talk—I was at a really low point—it was just like, ‘I’m here with my team and I’m pushing my limits and I’m seeing what’s possible for me.’ And that’s so exciting.

I would just tell myself ‘every step you take is a step you don’t have to take again.’ So I was just like, ‘I’m doing it. I’m slowly working towards that finish line, step by step.’ It was so funny because even when I was deeply uncomfortable, I never actually thought about quitting, which I thought I would. It was more just like I’m so uncomfortable, but I know I can if I just keep moving. Even if I’m slowing down, even if I’m not even able to run, I have to just power hike this section. I’m still moving towards my goal. I’m in the process of getting there, and that’s exciting in and of itself.

I kind of wanted to set up a charcuterie board of the trail world and try different things because they were all so different, right? Broken Arrow is a huge festival and it was a multi-day thing, so oh my gosh, what is day three gonna feel like? Can I even run downhill on day three?

And then Sierre-Zinal is so historic, and it was such a cool course. It was beautiful, and it was like experiencing a very classic “short” trail race, right? I was like, ‘this is not short.’ It took me 3 hours, but it was so cool to experience.

And then going into the 100 miler, it was different and more of a backyard format. Or not a backyard in terms of the laps, but like there was no award ceremony. It wasn’t about winning. It was just about doing it, and I love that. That is so aligned with how I feel about racing. It’s like, ‘No, we don’t really care who wins. We just want everyone to challenge themselves and hopefully make their goal of crossing the finish line.’ And that was so cool for me.

And so getting to be a part of each of these events, I got to experience so many different angles of the trail world and meet so many people. And for me, that was a big thing, too: feeling the sense of community that was around every single race and making new friends and trying something new. That was very cool.

No, I definitely am excited to do more. I don’t know what that’s gonna look like yet, but I feel like just getting to be involved in this world is so cool and so exciting. So, I’m sort of now in the phase of like, ‘OK, I feel like I’m bouncing back with 100. Like, my body’s coming back, and now I can start dreaming and scheming and brainstorming, like what else do I want to do? What else is out there? What excites me? What feels like the appropriate challenge for this phase of my life?’ Yeah, I’m trying to figure it all out.

I think the biggest thing was in training, like listening to my body. So I stopped wearing a heart rate monitor like five or six years ago, and it was really about being in tune and listening to my body and figuring out where I can push. What does it feel like when I’m riding that line of level three, and what are the signals in my body when I’ve gone over that line and I need to pull it back?

And so really trying to deeply understand how I feel, and I feel like that’s helped me steer away from injuries too, because I’m not relying on metrics. I want to feel how my body feels and respond to that and act on those feelings.I think that’s something I’m taking with me because I’m well aware now that running can really beat you up in a different way. Even listening to my body and learning how much can I eat while I’m running because your stomach is a washing machine and that does not happen in cross-country skiing.

I think it was really exciting in my final years of cross-country skiing, learning more about high-carb fueling and having all these great products come on board. Because in a ski race, let’s say a 50-kilometer race, you come through a feed zone, but you have gloves and your hands are in poles, so you are not like ripping open a gel. You’ll end up stabbing yourself in the face. And so what you do is you tuck your poles under your armpits and you grab the feed bottle, which is usually an actual baby bottle with the lid taken off, from a coach who cannot run with you, they have to just stand there and hold it by the rim. So you grab it while you are gliding quite quickly. You down it so you get like a few good sips, and then you have to chuck the bottle on the side and keep moving. And so having really high carb drink mixes where you can, if you only can get a few mouthfuls, you need them to count, and so having these was huge. Because before it’d be like, ‘I guess we’ll boil down Coke to de-fizz it, and that’s what you can have.’ But it  just wasn’t high carb enough, and the electrolyte balance might not have been great.

Now there’s so many options, and that really changed the way I could race. And so now, in trail racing, there’s all these different gels. You can find the one that works for you. There’s all these different mixes. You can find the amount of salt that works for you. That’s been really cool. Being able to tailor it. I feel like 15 years ago, there weren’t that many options. Now having more options is power.

I do get scared. It’s funny. I just saw on the elevator this morning a woman was wearing glitter, and I was like, ‘Yes!’ That was my whole thing through my ski career. And it came out of being scared and being nervous. And I feel like people don’t always know that that’s the origin. But I would get so nervous for races, and a little bit of nerves is great. It means you care. If you’re not nervous for a race, it’s sort of like, ‘Why am I doing this?’ You know, then it’s time to maybe examine, do I really care about what I’m doing?

Like with any work project, any life thing, I think that a little bit of nerves is super healthy. It also brings out the adrenaline and it tells your body, ‘I am ready to perform.’ But I would get nervous to the point where I’m stealing all my energy, and so it was hard to take yourself too seriously when you’re actually just covered in glitter. And so I would put on the sparkles as this promise to myself, like, ‘Hey, I get to be here. I get to do this. I got to sign up for this. That’s amazing. I have an opportunity to go out there and do my best at a sport that I love with a team that I love, and that’s really cool.’ And so the glitter was my pre-race ritual of ‘I’m going to go out there and have fun and remember to smile at the start because I’m so lucky to get to do this.’ Because sport is ultimately in the entertainment category. It is literally fun and games.

At the end of the day, yes, there’s a lot of pressure. There can be expectations. There can be a lot of lights. A lot of people are watching you, but you get to do this. You get to challenge yourself and see what’s possible. And that, in and of itself, is such an amazing opportunity.

#8276. Seven of the World’s Most Indulgent Après Spots

Under the sun-drenched, south-facing slope of the Matterhorn, après-ski tastes different—like homegrown Alpine herbal Génépy liqueur, Italian grappa, cloves, and orange zest all mixed with coffee.

This local mountain drink has been passed around the table for centuries in a multi-spouted little goblet fit for a hobbit, chiseled from a local walnut tree. But to sip from the Friendship Cup, or “Coppa dell’Amicizia”, you’ll need to drive two hours northwest of Milan or ski 14 miles on one of the world’s longest interconnected trails, leaving Zermatt’s vertical terrain, to cross into the Italian border recently redrawn by climate change.

You’ll know you’ve arrived in Italy’s Breuil-Cervinia when you pass directly beneath the Alps’ famous Toblerone-shaped peak (even after it was kicked off the candy bar wrapper).

Here in northwest Italy’s Aosta Valley, at the base inside VRetreats’ Zéro Lounge Bar & Bistrò, over affordable polenta, mountain cheese, and speck, the Friendship Cup is still rounding the table—always counterclockwise and never placed back down until every drop is gone. That would be bad luck.

“Its purpose is to bring friends together on the slopes,” says Daniel Menabreaz, manager of VRetreats Cervino Hotel, home of Zero Lounge, where guests can sip from the Friendship Cup while gazing out a wall of windows at the Matterhorn. “For our mountain community, where solidarity has always been an important value, it has become a genuine symbol of local identity.”

Skiers have been warming up with drinks and snacks after a day on the slopes ever since, toasting their survival in 19th-century Norway. Après-ski was popularized in Chamonix over “vin chaud” (mulled wine) paired with Chartreuse from Carthusian monks, and with the evolution of skiing came distinct regional après traditions. Today, after sizing up the vertical drop and sending it down the chute, the surest way to get to know a ski area is still celebrating like the locals.

Hot Take: Après Should Only Be For Those Who Ski

“Après-ski traditions are part of what gives each ski destination its own personality. They offer a window into a resort’s history, from local food and drink to the people who built the mountain community,” says Dana Zapfel, curator and director of collections for the Colorado Snowsports Museum in Vail.

Passing around the Friendship Cup in Italy, table dancing in ski boots in Austria, soaking in a Japanese onsen, or sharing a gourd of yerba mate around an Argentinian fire pit—this is what après-ski looks like around the world.

Imagine huddling around a backcountry fire pit in Patagonia. The kettle is steaming. The wind is whipping. Someone passes you a hollowed-out gourd filled with bright grassy green dried tea leaves, no booze involved. No one’s in a hurry. You’re still riding the natural high of taking turns overlooking sub-Antarctic ocean passages at the edge of the world.

Yerba mate’s earthy, bitter flavors have gotten skiers through the shortest, coldest days at the southern tip of Tierra del Fuego. They’re also a constant at Cerro Castor in Ushuaia, Argentina—and at the largest lift-served ski resort in the southern hemisphere, Cerro Catedral in San Carlos de Bariloche.

This Argentinian ritual started over 1,000 years ago with the region’s indigenous Guaraní people and was later carried by the gauchos through the plains and mountaineers looking for connection on the trail. Today, with the gourds in the backcountry, it’s also consumed via thermos cups in the chairlift line or while admiring the granite spires and sprawling glacial lakes (with a nibble of Argentinian chocolate and churros to cut the bitter taste).

On the same side of the Continental Divide, but worlds away from warm tea leaves and metal straws, is the parking lot at Arapahoe Basin.

Like many Colorado ski resorts, A-Basin was developed in the mid-20th century by 10th Mountain Division vet (Larry Jump with Olympic skier Frederick “Sandy” Schauffler), and while many of the other resorts just got bougier, A-Basin stayed true to its purpose.

This no-frills skier’s mountain is always one of the first to open and among the last to close out North America’s season, making the high-altitude spring ski party a non-negotiable. The question, with no slopeside accommodations, was how. In the 1980s, skiers pulled out their folding chairs and tables, popped up their tents and fired up the grills, in bathing suits no less. It’s been shot-skis all around at the bottom of the slope in the Early Riser parking lot, affectionately known as the Beach, ever since.

If A-Basin’s “Beach” out west is for tailgating, the East Coast Beach was made for reggae. Since 1988, when the spring snow begins to melt, die-hards have come out to play at the base of Sugarloaf for the annual Reggae Festival. This season’s festival will take place April 9-11, 2027.

Expect this massive mountain block party to fill up with “Loafers,” aka die-hard Sugarloaf skiers decked out in Pan-African red, gold, green, and black, neon tie-dyes and retro onesies—beach ball in one hand, can of official Orono Brewing Company Reggae Fest in the other.

From the mid-mountain stage at Bullwinkle’s Lodge (and a brand-new ice igloo inspired by Sunday River) to late-night bands at the Widowmaker and King Pine Room, this one’s for the rain-or-shine crowd.

In Japan, après-ski brings unmatched coziness. About three hours northwest of Tokyo in the Japanese Alps, on the main island of Honshu, skiers warm their sore muscles by baring it all (nudity required) in 13 natural hot springs inside bathhouses, known as onsen. This once-sacred bathing ritual, which starts from the chairlift, has been happening here for over twelve hundred years, since long before Nozawa Onsen Snow Resort opened in 1924.

After soaking it all up, walk the narrow cobblestone lantern-lit streets past steaming hot water channels to stop for sake in izakaya pubs—and if you’re feeling really rejuvenated, keep it going at traditional late-night karaoke and midnight ramen right there in the village.

With a 3,560-foot vertical drop and 400-plus inches of seasonal deep powder, skiing never felt better.

Whether you’re 22 or 72, table dancing in your ski boots in St. Anton’s MooserWirt (or neighboring Krazy Kanga) is unmatched, mostly because everyone’s dancing together. This is the world’s foremost legendary ski bar for good reason, beer consumption aside. With 23 miles of underground tubing pumping beer into the MooseWirt’s seven bars for 2,000 thirsty skiers a day—it’s no surprise, St. Anton claims Austria’s highest beer sales per square foot.

There are more important things to celebrate here, though. St. Anton am Arlberg is, of course, famously home to one of the oldest ski clubs and the most famous ski school in the world, where the father of modern skiing, Hannes Schneider, first taught the stem Christie ski method, the same instructional ways still used today.

Ride the chairlift over the Stuben hamlet where Schneider grew up in 1890, fuel up on a mid-mountain lunch at Valluga View, get up the nerve to ride the tin can gondola originally built in 1955 up to the summit for views of five countries, ski down for eight miles (but only with a certified mountain guide). And by the time you reach the bottom of Piste 50, you’ll hear the thumping—not of the bass, but from the stomping ski boots on the picnic tables (good thing they’re bolted down).

Somewhere between a simple mug of mulled mountain wine at a post-war ski gathering and the invasion of Hollywood and global billionaires, things got fancy in Courchevel, France.

Built on empty cow pastures to boost the economy, the resort made room to grow by design and kept getting more extravagant. Today, you have your pick of all the Michelin-starred restaurants and lavish slope-side parties in private chalets and five-star hotels—or maybe you’re after an ultra-luxury cigar from The Winston Club. Sink into the leather armchair next to a crackling wood fireplace by the window with sweeping summit views; then let the cigar sommelier select a rare Cuban to pair with your vintage cognac and finish off the day.

And, if you dream big enough, you might make it back for the 2030 Winter Olympics (Alpes 2030), when Courchevel becomes an official host once again.

#8275. Shah Daulat, a Celebrated Alpinist Who Summited K2, Dies at 31

Shah Daulat, 31, was raised in the mountains of Shimshal, a remote village in Pakistan’s Hunza Valley that has encouraged and supported generations of the country’s strongest climbers. In his early years of being a professional guide with the Karakoram Mountain Guides Association, Daulat climbed four of the world’s 8,000-meter peaks, cementing his legacy as one of Pakistan’s rising alpinists.

“His journey from a mountain guide to climbing some of the world’s most challenging peaks is something our family is incredibly proud of,” Ibadat said. “He dedicated his life to the mountains and was deeply passionate about climbing.”

Daulat began working as a guide in 2022, and his progression onto the world’s highest peaks came quickly. That year, he summited K2, at 8,611 meters the second-highest mountain in the world. In 2023, he climbed 8,126-meter Nanga Parbat without supplemental oxygen, followed by Gasherbrum II in 2024. In 2025, he summited Gasherbrum I, again without supplemental oxygen, marking his fourth 8,000-meter summit in as many years. That same year, he also climbed Laila Peak, a 6,096-meter mountain in Pakistan’s Hushe Valley.

But his life in the mountains extended far beyond expedition climbing. He was a skier, too, competing at Malam Jabba in northern Pakistan in 2022. And though his career took him to some of the highest vistas in the world, it was on a much smaller objective, close to home, that he passed.

On February 6, 2026, Daulat was ice climbing near Khyber village in Gojal, Hunza, when he fell nearly 400 meters. Local volunteers recovered his body, which was later returned to his home village of Shimshal for burial.

After his death, Daulat’s cousin, pioneering Pakistani mountaineer Samina Baig, remembered both what he had accomplished in a remarkably short climbing career and the person behind those achievements. “Shah Daulat was a true gem in our family—a cherished younger brother (cousin) taken from us far too soon,” Baig wrote in a Facebook tribute. “A young mountaineer, he achieved so much in such a short life, touching many hearts with his courage and gentle spirit.

“May he rest in peace among the mountains he loved,” she continued. “He will forever remain in our hearts, remembered with love and quiet pride.”

In September, the artist Iowna Chichowich installed a life-sized memorial sculpture of Daulat near the Khyber Ice Wall, which has been renamed the Shah Daulat Ice Wall.

#8273. Editor’s Letter: Why Do Hard Things Outside? Our Outsiders of the Year Answer

Anyone who does hard things outside has heard it. Why climb a mountain that’s already been climbed? Why run 253 miles across a desert? To test the limits of human potential is the tidy answer. The real one, as our Outsiders of the Year show, shifts like snow on a big face: it’s different for everyone, and never quite the same twice.

This year Alex Honnold free soloed a 1,667-foot skyscraper live on Netflix, after being explained away as a brain-scan curiosity for two decades. Now 40, with two preschoolers, he fits climbing in where he can. Some days that means getting up at 2 a.m. to climb a thousand-foot granite wall to still make it home for dinner. Why bother? “In some ways, climbing is my only opportunity to feel like I’m good at something,” he tells Features Editor Frederick Dreier. Any parent who has squeezed in a run between school pickups knows the feeling.

Jim Morrison and his partner Hilaree Nelson shared a dream no one had pulled off: to climb Everest’s North Face and ski it back down. In 2022, Nelson died on Manaslu, and Morrison swore off the mountains. Then his dog started pulling him back up the trail, a little higher every day. In 2025, with Jimmy Chin filming beside him for Everest: The Other Side, Morrison skied 9,000 feet off the top of the world. At the bottom, he screamed, “That one’s for you, Hil.”

Not everyone on Everest gets to ask why. Sherpas still take the biggest risks so others can reach the top. This spring, Hillary Dawa Sherpa, a 57-year-old cook, was pushed toward the summit when his outfitter came up a guide short. Descending with eight empty oxygen bottles (lose one and he’d be docked $250), he ran out of air and was assumed dead. Six days later, he dragged himself out of the Khumbu Icefall on a broken leg. He’d only gone because someone else’s summit needed him.

For Christina Koch, the answer was bigger than herself. In April, she flew around the moon on Artemis II under a patch her crew designed so “A II” read as “all.” When she heard the whole planet was watching, she cried, and in zero gravity, the tears had nowhere to fall.

Rachel Entrekin’s answer is the hardest-won of all. As a teenager, she nearly didn’t survive. In treatment for an eating disorder, she learned a rule she still runs by: do the very thing you least want to do. This year she ran 253 miles across Arizona and became the first woman to win the Cocodona outright. “Running helps me practice who I want to be when things get tough,” she says.

Adventure has never had a bigger audience. Millions watched Honnold’s climb in real time, and this fall, Everest is all over movie screens. Almost none of those viewers will ski Everest or solo a skyscraper. But every one of those moments sends someone out the door to find their own answer. Ask anyone at a trailhead on a Sunday morning why they came: to do something hard, to carry someone with them, to feel small in front of something vast, to become who they want to be.

The Northflag gets that the best travel gear does its job without asking for attention. The name nods to the 1950s British North Greenland Expedition, where the explorers wore Tudors, but its smartest feature is modern: a true GMT, so you can set local time the moment you land and still know the time back home. It’ll keep running for almost three days after you take it off, and it looks as right at a trailhead as at the dinner table.

Every trip has a weather day, and this is the shoe I pack for it. The Gore-Tex membrane keeps my feet dry, and the gravel-tuned outsole and bouncy foam handle pavement and light trail equally well. I’ve logged about 50 miles of Italy’s Via Francigena in it, both hiking and running, and ran all over London and Paris. Best part: it doesn’t look ridiculous with civilian clothes. One shoe, three jobs, and more room in my carry-on.

This article is from the Winter 2026 issue of Outside magazine. To receive the print magazine, become an Outside+ member here.

#8271. Are Apex Ski Boots Any Good? A Bootfitter’s Honest Review.

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

Are Apex ski boots any good? A bootfitter skis the Antero VS Carbon at Kirkwood and explains exactly who they suit, and what you give up in feel on snow. (Photo: Jake Stern)

Overview: Apex ski boots pair a snowboard-style boot with a plastic-and-carbon exoskeleton that snaps into ski bindings. They suit skiers who want comfort and a few easy laps, including older skiers and those with mobility issues. The tradeoff is feel: a bootfitter who tested the Antero VS Carbon at Kirkwood found it carves when you angulate, but left him disconnected from the ski, especially in bumps.

Unloading Chair 6 at Kirkwood, I hesitated before dropping in. Sure, I’d skied the liftline bumps a dozen times without a second thought, but then I was wearing my own boots. I looked down at the contraptions buckled to my feet, a maze of tubular webbing, carbon cages and… snowboard boots, and sighed. I had promised my editor I’d test these Apex ski boots, and you can’t do that in your living room.

Founded in Colorado in 2006, Apex Ski Boots reimagined what a ski boot could be. They paired a snowboard boot with a plastic-and-carbon exoskeleton that snaps into ski bindings, purporting to offer comfort, warmth, and exceptional power transfer. Apex has three models: the Crestone VS, the Blanca VS, and the Antero VS Carbon, which I tested. After most of a decade of rabid reader requests to test Apex boots for SKI’s boot guides, we finally relented. I went to Kirkwood to see what all the fuss was about.

Pros and Cons + Soft boot is more comfortable than a rigid, traditional ski boot + Easy entry + You can shed the exoskeleton and walk around in the soft boot after skiing – Complicated to buckle up – Lacks precision and support on snow

I fit boots for a handful of years and you’re bound to pick up some biases. The crusty old sages who gift you their knowledge will also make sure their prejudices become yours. Van Osgood, a mentor of mine and an artist with a dremel, is a dyed-in-the-wool Apex Ski Boots hater. I lost count of the times I heard him describe making a turn in the hybrid boots: “First, you think about turning, then, a second later, the ski starts to tip, then, a second later, the ski starts to come around,” he’d say. “Think about that in tight trees.”

But I slowly overcame that bias, simply by watching skiers come into the shop carrying those boots. Older skiers, folks with mobility issues, and people who just wanted to take a few laps in comfort loved the things. I began to associate them with people who didn’t necessarily charge, but who loved the sport just as much as I did. The strong caveat here is an old friend, Tommy Ellingson, who can throw a cork 7 in Apexes, but I firmly believe he can do that in literally anything.

I wanted to see how the slander, hearsay, and praise actually shook out on snow—especially after the Apex rep talked up the Antero VS Carbon as made for “the double blacks and beyond.” I sized down aggressively to match my alpine boots—I measure just shy of a 28.5 but comfortably wear a 26.5—so the rep set me up with a heat mold and then told me to go skiing. Where better to test the double-black diamond performance claim than Kirkwood?

I didn’t head straight for Y-Spine. Instead, I dialed in the snowboard boots at the car and walked the chassis over to Chair 11 to get them on a groomer. The first thing I noticed is that to get the boot to feel even remotely snug, I had to dial in the buckles so tightly that the boots were much less comfortable than my daily drivers, the Armada AR ONE 130. I felt pressure points on my instep that made me loosen the dials for lack of circulation, which left some lateral play in my forefoot.

On snow, I decided I had no choice but to trust the boot. I remember thinking before tipping my skis: either this works, or I crash, but I have to try. It turns out I was being melodramatic. If you angulate, the boot tips the ski and you will carve a turn. That said, I’ve never felt so disconnected from my skis. I felt like I was floating far above the ski and couldn’t perceive any rebound out of the turn. I knew I was making an arc by looking down and seeing my progress, but there was zero proprioception to speak of—I didn’t have a clue where my body was in space.

Skiing bumps was an even stranger experience. The skis turned, and I could pivot against the bumps and make it down just fine, but turns felt incredibly vague, like I was skiing bumps more by memory than by feel—the boots took away the sensation of the snow underfoot.

I went back to my car after six laps to think. How did I want to relate this story to the world? To be clear, I had no interest in dunking on Apex. For a long time now, Apex boots have filled a niche for skiers who love the sport but have no interest or ability to buckle themselves into a plastic shell. And judging by online reviews, there are plenty of skiers who genuinely love these ski boots.

But with the advent of boots like the Rossignol Vizion and Atomic Nexus, I’m at a bit of a loss for where Apex now fits in the market. Because there are now high-performance options for folks with mobility issues, and those boots are far easier to get in and out of than a snowboard boot with multiple BOA dials inside a chassis with multiple buckles. And those boots are far more comfortable, as I find a squishy ski boot liner beats the stout snowboard liner—though I imagine the less “high-performance” models of the Apex offer better comfort.

What I’m left with is that somewhere out there exists a market for Apex ski boots, but I think that market is shrinking as new boot tech arrives each year. I’m happy to say that I gave them an honest shot, and they’re not for me. Apex boots make sense for skiers who want a few comfortable laps and don’t care about precision or feeling the snow underfoot; if you ski for feel, skip them. But I have the utmost respect for anyone who wants to get on snow and thinks this is the best option for them. I’ll leave you with proof that they carve, though I won’t be winning any beer-league GS events in Apex boots.

#8270. The Sun Never Shines in This Norwegian Ice Climbing Mecca

Heike Schmitt leads the crux pitch of ‘Juvsøyla’ (WI5/6), one of Rjukan’s crown jewels. (Photo: Jonas Paulsson)

Norway in February is a lot like what you’d expect. Snow and ice-covered roads. Short, cold days. Long, cold nights. Endless forested mountains with sharply serrated interludes.

But I did not expect there to be so much ice.

In Rjukan, a town of 3,000 located three hours from the capital of Oslo, there are over 200 ice and mixed routes, up to 800 meters long, ranging from mellow WI2 flows to some of the hardest pure ice in Europe. Many of the routes are multi-pitch, and many can be accessed within 10 minutes of walking from your car.

As someone who lives in the ice mecca of the Canadian Rockies, I thought I’d seen what a “high concentration” of ice means. But drive through the tight, shaded valley of Rjukan in February and you’ll kink your neck eight ways at once trying to glimpse all the ice available to you. Crucially, there is a nearly endless supply of ice for beginners and intermediates—a WI2-4 climber’s delight.

I visited Rjukan in February 2025 to attend the Norrøna Ice Festival. Climbers from all over came to sample this world-class area—Italy, Poland, the United States, Scotland—and the Europeans in particular remarked at how reliable Norwegian ice seemed to be relative to the rest of the continent. It makes sense: Norway is famously cold, famously wet, and, for roughly half the year, the town of Rjukan sees exactly zero direct sunlight. That is a sure-fire recipe for fantastic ice climbing.

If you yearn to feel some sunlight on your face, drop in to the Rjukan town square on a clear day. In 2013, the municipality installed three giant mirrors on the north side of the valley, which are powered by solar and rotate to reflect the sun’s rays down into town.

I’ve been to a number of climbing festivals over the years—from Squamish to Spain, New Hampshire to Norway—and I found the Norrøna fest to be refreshingly unique. Rjukan is a bit of a backwoods town and just getting there is a minor hassle—especially for the many participants who are internationals and fly into Oslo. As a result, Norrøna offers a “full package” festival experience. The organizers told me and every other participant how to get from our arrival gates to their head office, fed us a three-course dinner, and let us climb at their gym (which rivals any mega gym I’ve ever visited), before schlepping us to Rjukan.

The “package” is certainly more expensive that bussing from Oslo, sleeping in a tent, and walking to each crag day after day, but, as one of the participants living in Italy pointed out to me, Norway is an expensive country to visit and organizing your own rental car, accommodation, and meals will shake out to nearly the same cost without the festival’s group rate. And, personally, I loved the camaraderie that developed between participants day after day, meal after meal.

Whether you’re considering visiting the Norrøna Ice Festival next year or just want to go experience this dark and dreamy valley of ice yourself, here are some tips I picked up from my trip.

Norway’s high-flow waterfalls, or fossen, are a sight to behold. But be warned, as I was by pro climber Matthias Scherer: these wet lines can be an absolute nightmare to descend, since freezing conditions will turn rappel ropes into thick, icy cables. Make sure to bring ropes with a fresh dry treatment.

#8269. This 30-Mile-Long Canyonlands Art Gallery Might Be Utah’s Best Backpacking Trip

When you think of ancient rock art, what comes to mind? Handprints? Stick figures? Maybe a long-limbed man holding something? For the most part, you’d be right. The petroglyphs and pictographs of the southwest are beautiful, but they aren’t known for their intricate details.

But there’s one canyon in Utah that blows those expectations out of the water.

Hidden deep inside Canyonlands National Park, Salt Creek Canyon holds some of the most impressive pictographs I’ve ever seen. Enormous human figures, elaborate patterns, and colorful paintings that have survived for hundreds of years. It’s an open-air art museum, and one that’s slowly weathering away.

And the museum doesn’t stop at rock art. There are Ancestral Puebloan granaries, settlers’ abandoned ranch buildings, and reminders of the conservationists who helped protect this landscape.

A walk through Salt Creek Canyon is a walk through history. Over two days and more than 30 miles, it became one of my biggest backpacking surprises of the year.

Trail: Salt Creek Trail + Angel Arch Detour Start: Cathedral Butte / Salt Creek Canyon Trailhead Finish: Cave Spring / Salt Creek Gate Distance: 30.78 miles (my GPS; mapped distance may differ) Elevation gain: 1,054 feet (my GPS) Type: Point-to-point, vehicle shuttle required Permits: Required for overnight trips Highlight: The All American Man pictograph

The trail begins high in the contested Bears Ears National Monument, in the shadow of Cathedral Butte. Typically, this is the sort of view you’d have to earn after hours of climbing. Instead, you start at the highest point, looking down into a canyon that stretches toward the horizon.

It’s mostly downhill from here, but don’t mistake that for easy. Thirty miles with a loaded backpack is still 30 miles, especially when much of it is through deep sand.

About two miles in, we crossed into Canyonlands National Park. My Gaia GPS map was littered with waypoints and “Don’t miss!” markers, the first of which were Kirk Spring and Kirk’s Cabin.

In an otherwise dusty landscape of sagebrush and juniper, a little oasis appeared. Reeds, cottonwoods, and bright green vegetation surrounded a small spring. We filtered some water and continued toward the cabin, an 1890s-era log home with a fieldstone chimney.

Outside the weathered log structure sat the wheels and axles of an old wagon. Inside, bear traps and antlers hung on the walls. It looked like something out of a history museum, only sandier, dustier, and considerably more authentic.

This was our first introduction to one of Salt Creek’s defining qualities: Layers of human history occupy nearly every corner of the canyon.

Long before ranchers arrived, Indigenous people—Ancestral Puebloans and Fremont, then Ute, Paiute, and Diné—lived, hunted, and farmed here. Later came European explorers, conservationists, and eventually backpackers like us. Different people, different centuries, but all drawn to the same remarkable place.

One of the biggest reasons was water. Unlike much of Canyonlands, Salt Creek supports a surprisingly lush corridor of vegetation, even in a dry year. We encountered several places to filter water, although sources became scarcer farther down the canyon. (Water here is seasonal and never guaranteed, so come prepared to carry plenty.)

Around mile six, a small spur trail led us beneath a sandstone overhang. Tucked into the alcove were several stone structures, likely granaries used by Ancestral Puebloan people to store their harvests. Just below them, dark-green vines spilled across the sand. They looked like squash plants, still thriving in the shadow of structures built centuries ago.

I’d come to Salt Creek expecting incredible rock art, but nothing prepared me for what we found around mile eight: The All American Man.

High inside a sandstone alcove stands a human-like figure, nearly life-size, painted in striking blue, white, and red. He appears to wear white boots, an elaborate headdress, and something resembling an American flag across his body.

For decades, the figure’s unusual appearance led some to question whether it was even ancient. Radiocarbon testing eventually confirmed its authenticity, suggesting it dates to around the 14th century. Standing below it, I found the whole thing almost impossible to believe. (Do yourself a favor: If you plan on hiking Salt Creek, don’t look up pictures of the All American Man beforehand. Let it surprise you.)

Not far beyond, we encountered another extraordinary panel near Four Faces Spring. Four enormous, intricately patterned faces stared out from beneath a sandstone alcove. Remnants of stone structures sat beneath them.

Who were these figures? Were they people, spirits, or something else entirely?

Their exact meaning remains uncertain, but the artwork survives, part of a cultural history that remains important to Indigenous communities today.

The farther we walked, the more the canyon changed.

Towering sandstone walls closed in around us. Willows, reeds, and cottonwoods transformed the dusty trail into something resembling a jungle. Small streams appeared beneath the vegetation.

Unfortunately, so did the mosquitoes. I’ve spent a lot of time hiking through the desert, but I’ve never encountered so many of the little suckers.

After miles of hiking, a soft rain finally brought some relief. A rainbow appeared against the red canyon walls just as we approached SC4, our reserved campsite for the evening.

At roughly mile 12, SC4 is the last of the four designated Salt Creek campsites when traveling north. It wasn’t quite halfway through our route, which meant we had an even longer second day ahead.

The next morning, we packed up and headed toward another of the canyon’s great attractions. Several miles off the main trail, at the end of a remote side canyon, stood Angel Arch.

Arches National Park may be famous for its sandstone formations, but Angel Arch can hold its own against just about anything you’ll find there.

Its massive sandstone opening rises roughly 135 feet high, with an unusual formation beside it resembling an angel leaning forward with folded wings. It’s an incredible sight, made even more impressive by the effort required to reach it. We were the only people there. In fact, we were the only hikers on the entire trail: We hadn’t seen a single other person or group. The detour added several miles to an already long day, but I’d do it again without hesitation.

Back on the main route, one more archaeological treasure awaited us: the Flying Carpet Panel. Like the All American Man and Four Faces, the artwork was enormous, with figures and intricate designs spread across the sandstone.

Then came the final miles. The beautiful canyon trail eventually gave way to a sandy four-wheel-drive road, where every step seemed to require twice the effort. After nearly 30 miles, walking through deep sand was just about the last thing my legs wanted to do.

Eventually, we reached a gate, a paved road, and the end of our journey.

As spectacular as the scenery was, what I’ll remember most about Salt Creek isn’t the canyon itself. It’s the people who called it home.

For centuries, Ancestral Puebloan communities farmed along the creek, stored food in cliffside granaries, and created artwork that still watches over the canyon today. Walking past these places, I couldn’t help thinking about how many people had traveled this same canyon before us. How many had looked up at those same cliffs, collected water from those same springs, or sheltered beneath those sandstone overhangs?

We spent two days here, carrying everything we needed on our backs. For others, this canyon was home. For a brief moment, we got to be part of its story too.

#8268. Lawmakers Move to Ban AI Data Centers on National Forests and Federal Land

Meta's 2.4-million-square-foot data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah. A new bill introduced in Congress would prohibit construction of data centers on federally managed public lands. (Photo: George Frey/Getty)

There’s a new plan in Washington to prohibit the construction of AI data centers on public lands.

On November 11, Oregon Representative Maxine Dexter introduced the Protecting Our Public Lands from Data Centers Act, which would ban new data centers on national forests and lands managed by the U.S. Department of the Interior.

The legislation, backed by 13 Democratic cosponsors, would also require federal land sold or transferred to return to government ownership if used for a data center without congressional authorization.

“Public lands belong in public hands and Oregonians must have a say before the federal government hands over millions of acres of public land managed by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) for data centers,” Dexter said in a November 11 press release. “These treasured lands are where people hunt, fish, hike and graze livestock. They are where wildlife habitat and our critical watersheds are protected. My bill keeps these lands safe from data centers now, and for the generations who come after us.”

The bill arrived just one day after the Interior Department published its strategic plan for fiscal years 2026 through 2030, which outlines proposals to sell federal land to states, local governments, and tribes, while expanding energy and infrastructure development to support growing demand from data centers.

The plan drew criticism from public lands advocates, including Tracy Stone-Manning, who led the BLM under President Joe Biden and now serves as president of the Wilderness Society.

“They want to sell it off for data centers. They want to sell it off to oil and gas companies,” Stone-Manning said in a November 14 NPR interview. “They want to sell it off because they don’t like the idea of the American public owning these lands.”

Throughout 2026 the Trump Administration has sought to build data centers on public lands. According to a November 6 investigation from ProPublica, the BLM is reviewing permit applications for approximately 15 data centers and 17 related infrastructure projects across six Western states. In its five-year strategic plan for public lands management, the DOI says it will find ways to address “the growing demand from Super Intelligence data centers.”

In July, Outside reported that the BLM approved plans for an 86-acre AI data center roughly ten miles from Lake Mead National Recreation Area in Nevada. An Interior Department appeals board has since paused the project for further review, ProPublica reported.

The rise of artificial intelligence and cloud-based computing has accelerated the need for these centers. But data centers can place significant demands on electricity and water supplies, and throughout 2026, the centers have grown unpopular with voters. A September report by Pew Research found that 54 percent of Americans found data centers to be bad for the environment, up from just 39 percent in January.

More municipalities have passed moratoriums on the construction of the data centers, leading officials to look to rural or backcountry settings for them. But the construction of the centers can disrupt wildlife habitat and restrict public access to formerly open land, according to the November 11 release.

“Data centers have no place on public lands,” said Randi Spivak of the nonprofit group Center for Biological Diversity in a release. “They’re water-guzzling, pollution-spewing facilities that turn lands meant for wildlife and recreation into corporate industrial sites.”

More recently, an interactive map covered by Outside identified at least 14 proposed data centers within ten miles of national park boundaries.

Dexter’s legislation has been referred to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture committees. The bill has no Republican cosponsors, and a similar measure introduced by Oregon Senator Ron Wyden was blocked by Republican Senator Rand Paul in September. No new restrictions have taken effect.

#8267. Escape Winter With These 6 Underrated Desert Trail Runs

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In his research for his upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” Andy Cochrane ran hundreds of trails across the U.S. These are his six favorites across the Southwest that come into season when most of the country is hibernating.

With all due respect to Presidential Traverse, Teton Crest, and Wonderland, the most sought-after one-day trail running route in the U.S. is the Grand Canyon Rim-to-Rim-to-Rim. Every spring and fall runners flock to Arizona to test their luck on this double lap of the big ditch, despite the National Park Service strongly advising against it. (Signs around the Grand Canyon warn of heat illness, elevation, and difficult evacs.)

Some have called R2R2R an obsession—while I’m not sure I would personally go that far, I do see the argument. I’ve run the route three times and each trip I find myself more enamored than the last. On my last visit in 2023, a peak autumn weekend with nearly perfect temps and all the water facets still running (the NPS shuts some of them down seasonally), I saw hundreds of runners attempting R2R2R. That’s a tiny fraction of the four and a half million people who visit the park each year, but very busy for a trail run.

However, that was before the closures. The North Rim of the Grand Canyon was shuttered for most of the 2025 season due to the Dragon Bravo Fire, which burned 149,000 acres and 118 buildings. Then, on August 29th, 2026, a flash flood struck Phantom Ranch at the bottom of the Grand Canyon, killing three and forcing 82 others to be evacuated by helicopter. Trail damage was widespread, taking out footbridges and much of the park’s water line. The North Kaibab Trail, parts of the Bright Angel and South Kaibab trails, and sections of the River Trail remain closed with no set date for reopening.

It’s getting colder and darker across most of the country. That means one thing: It’s desert season. In lieu of a double dip into the Grand Canyon—and to open your mind to the endless possibilities elsewhere—I’ve compiled a list of my six favorite trails across the American Southwest. All of them are in my upcoming book, “The 50 Classic Trail Runs of America” (which you can pre-order now!). They cover six different states and four unique desert ecosystems, so there is plenty of variety to choose from.

Unlike the rocky singletrack of the Northeast, the forested trails of the upper Midwest, or the alpine ridges of the West, running across the Southwest desert is a singular experience. Limited shade, even less water, and direct solar radiation create obvious hydration challenges. The temperature swings dramatically from near freezing overnight to scorching heat midday. The trails themselves are a mix of surfaces, from soft sand to loose scree to firm slickrock, with many—including the ones listed below—being very remote.

Beyond the physical experience, running in arid environments carries a different emotion, too. I often find myself in a quiet and contemplative mental space, passing by ancient saguaros, joshua trees, and prickly pears while trying to stay alert for subtle movements of rattlesnakes, lizards, and coyotes. Running in the desert is, simultaneously, the antidote to life’s complexity and a plague of endless possibility.

There are four distinct desert ecosystems in the U.S. The northernmost is the Great Basin, which covers most of Nevada and parts of neighboring states, making it the largest desert in the country. With frigid winters, it’s filled with sagebrush instead of cacti. Just south is the Mojave, the smallest of the four, which is home to Death Valley and Joshua Tree. Further south is the Sonoran, the “green desert,” with large saguaros and rainfall in both summer and winter. Last, the Chihuahuan, covers West Texas and southern New Mexico, and is known for succulents like Agave, Yucca, and Creosote.

Hidden in one of North America’s most remote national parks, Big Bend, the Outer Mountain Loop is a 32-mile circuit featuring a stark ecological contrast between the Chihuahuan Desert and the high-alpine Chisos Mountains. Beginning and ending in the Chisos Basin, a sky-island that’s home to rare species like the Colima Warbler, the trail plunges down stone steps and rolls across the sun-scorched flats of the Dodson Trail before making a grueling 3,000-foot final ascent up Blue Creek Canyon. Early Spanish explorers called this isolated region El Despoblado.

Why I love it: Getting to experience both sky islands and the solitude of the Chihuahuan desert.

Spanning 39 miles from the edge of the Navajo Nation to the Grand Canyon’s South Rim, the Little to Big Colorado route is the less conventional way to explore one of the country’s most popular national parks. Tracing the historic Hopi salt journeys, the route plunges down Bekihatso Wash, follows the Little Colorado to its confluence with the Colorado River, passes sacred sites, scrambles obstacles like the Papago Wall, and passes by billion-year-old rock. With a 4,700-foot grind up the New Hance Trail at the end, it’s just as challenging and rewarding as rim-to-rim-to-rim.

Why I love it: It’s so close to the most famous one day trail route in the country, but still unheard of.

Crossing the national park from east to west, this 37-mile rolling route passes two distinct deserts—the higher Mojave and the lower Sonora—as you wander by long shadows of Yucca brevifolia (Joshua trees) and massive, weathered granite batholiths. Championed by the activist Minerva Hamilton Hoyt after decades of cattle grazing and mining exploitation, this sandy sanctuary strips away the crowds, offering sheer solitude as runners cross ancient mountain passes, gaze down at the dark expanse of the Salton Sea, and experience a desert communion.

Why I love it: it’s the one place in America that feels straight out of a Dr. Seuss book.

One of the most remote routes we considered for the book, this 64-mile trek traces the ridgeline of the Toiyabe Range. Like Outer Mountain, this area is a sky island, a rare ecosystem in which the valley below is a scorching hot desert, but the trail itself is a lush forest of aspen and bristlecone pines, some 3,000 years old. Despite being Nevada’s longest named trail, Toiyabe is off-trail in nature, with significant routefinding and some sections of unrunnable terrain.

Why I love it: Remote and rugged, it’s a good test of navigation and alpine movement of all sorts.

Perched above Albuquerque, this 26-mile trail follows a limestone ridge along the backbone of the Sandia Mountains, with 360-degree views of the Rio Grande Valley below. Sandia is Spanish for watermelon, named after the ridge’s unique sunset alpenglow that turns the cliffs deep pink, with green conifers on top representing the rind. The trail features wildflowers, ponderosas, spruce, and white fir, and can be accessed via an aerial tramway, providing easy access without sacrificing its rugged, aesthetic appeal.

Why I love it: Quick and easy access paired with absolutely beautiful sunsets.

Winding through one of Southern Utah’s most distinctive landscapes, the 30-mile Bryce Canyon Traverse links the heavily trafficked northern amphitheater where thousands of hoodoos, rock fins, and natural arches create a natural maze with the primitive Under the Rim Trail to the south. Crossing a geological marvel shaped by erosion and freeze-thaw cycles over millions of years, the traverse is the best way to see it all. Heading southbound allows runners to catch sunrise over the spires before descending into remote backcountry, which is the direction we recommend.

Why I love it: There’s no place in the world with the same density or volume of hoodoos.

Desert running presents many challenges that the Mafate X can handle. Deserts are often oven-hot, so having a woven, high-airflow upper is ideal. They are rocky and filled with pokey things, so having a taller stack with soft PEBA foam is a bonus. They are loose, so having Vibram lugs adds a level of stability and confidence. And, with uneven ground, a wide base makes your feet feel much more planted, too.

On long, sweaty days, sunscreen only goes so far. I take extra precaution and wear a Tahoe sun hoody, which delivers UPF 50+ protection against harsh UV rays, paired with a light polyester-spandex knit that wicks sweat off my skin and dries quickly. And, integrated thumbholes and a fitted hood keep my hands and neck completely covered without restricting movement.

For most desert runs I recommend stashing water the day before, but if you aren’t able to, having an extra large running pack is key. Kiprun’s 10L has room for a bladder in the back and two flasks up front, which is ideal for long desert stretches. The harness keeps the pack secure and large front pockets make it easy to access your phone, electrolytes, snacks, or sunscreen on the go.

My favorite drink mix, Fuel combines essential electrolytes like sodium, potassium, and magnesium to replace minerals lost in heavy sweat. It tastes good, prevents cramps, and the added zinc supports fluid retention in hot conditions. Using a low-GI carb from beet sugar, it also provides steady energy without blood sugar spikes or crashes, which is great for longer days.

#8265. The Ephemeral Global Climbing School Amid China’s Epic Limestone

On October 22, hundreds of climbers of all skill levels descended upon Yangshuo, China, for the long-awaited  2026 Arc’teryx Climb Academy. Participants say the remarkable thing about the weekend wasn’t just the climbing or even the new skills they learned—it was the magic of the remote, fantastical landscape, and the opportunity to connect with people across cultures and continents.

The Arc’teryx Climb Academy is a roving international climbing school—and one that offers some of the most advanced mountain education in the world. Since 2007, academies have been held in global climbing epicenters like Squamish, Chamonix, and Mammoth Lakes. Some focus on climbing while others offer backcountry or freeride skiing education. Each installment is a complex undertaking, bringing together world-class guides and athletes to pass on their knowledge in a highly efficient, structured format. Dozens of courses—ranging from alpine overnights to big wall workshops to mental resilience clinics—are designed to meet participants where they’re at. At each academy, students can learn skills from scratch, drill fundamentals, or significantly boost their skills, even within just a few days of instruction.

While there are tons of events in the climbing universe, Arc’teryx Climb Academies stand out for just how seamlessly they’re run and how well integrated they are into the local community. Unlike some climbing festivals, which tend to put more emphasis on socialization than education, Arc’teryx has figured out how to nail both without compromising either. All day long, participants of every skill level take hands-on courses on some of the best rock in the world, each one packed with pro-level hacks, technique drills, and actionable tips for continuing your education after the trip ends. Each evening, a five-star lineup of films, speakers, music, and parties makes it impossible to tear yourself away. Every chapter of the event buoys you along to the next. The weekend passes in a flash. And you return home with more phone numbers, more new climbing partners, and more stoke than you could have imagined possible.

In 2023, the series brought this special blend of inspiration and education to the limestone cliffs of Yangshuo, China—and the event was a runaway hit. In 2024, the Academy returned with even more courses crafted specifically for the local community, including rescue and evacuation clinics tailored to China’s uniquely rocky landscapes. The 2026 Academy further expanded the course menu, offering beginner trad clinics, bolting workshops, and masterclasses in big wall climbing. Over four days, hundreds of climbers participated in 37 clinics at more than a dozen crags across the stunning Guangxi region. It was the region’s biggest Arc’teryx Climb Academy yet.

While many of the Academy’s participants came specifically to experience Yangshuo’s world-renowned karst spires, the crags aren’t just a backdrop here; they’re the heart of a thriving and longstanding community of climbers, route developers, and outdoor businesses. Since international climbers first arrived in the late 1980s, the zone has grown to nearly 2,000 routes across 74 crags on world-class limestone.

“Yangshuo means a lot to me,” says Peng Zhou, renowned Chinese mountaineer and Arc’teryx athlete. “I completed both my first 5.12 and 5.14 routes here, and it has left me with many wonderful memories.” He loves getting an opportunity to share this place with newcomers; it’s one of the reasons he comes back to teach year after year.

Given Yangshuo’s robust existing climbing scene, the event offers more cultural exchange than top-down discourse. Here, international visitors learn just as much from their Chinese counterparts as locals learn from the global pros.

Take it from Arc’teryx athlete Quentin Roberts. This year, he taught his third Yangshuo Big Wall Climbing clinic in a row. Each time, he’s astonished by how much the climbing community has grown since his last visit. “Every year I feel like I have had to level up to meet the growing ambitions and skills of the participants,” he says. “It’s exciting to see how eager everyone is.”

But for Roberts, the best part about climbing in China is the profound and indescribable warmth of the Yangshuo community.

“We always have a big, Chinese-style, round-table dinner with all the instructors before the event,” he says. It’s an evening filled with laughter between old friends. Jokes and stories fly across the table like sparks, and Roberts leaves feeling filled up at a soul level. “Many of the people in that room are at the forefront of climbing in China. It’s special to feel that sense of family, and to see the passion everyone has for what they’re doing.”

It’s that sense of connection that makes the Yangshuo event—and the other installments of the Arc’teryx Climb Academy—so invaluable.

“Coming to China over the years and connecting with people through climbing has really reinforced something I believe deeply: we are all more similar than we are different,” says Roberts. “Climbing has an incredible ability to bring people together. Sharing a rope, trusting one another, sharing our experiences—those connections transcend language and culture.”

Arc’teryx is a Canadian company based in the Coast Mountains. Our design process is connected to the real world, focused on delivering unrivaled durability and performance in extreme conditions. Our products are distributed through over 160 branded stores and more than 2,400 retail locations worldwide. We are problem solvers, evolving and searching for a better way to deliver resolved, minimalist designs. Good design that matters makes lives better.

#8264. Giant November Waves Threaten Surfers, Swimmers, and Spectators Along California’s Coast

Powerful waves crash against Pacifica Pier in Pacifica, California, on November 14, 2026, as large Pacific swells batter the state's coastline. (Photo: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images)

Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz.

In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI.

“I’ve seen seasons start off with a bang like this, but we’ve never had this type of impact so immediate,” Ernst Bauen, operations division chief for the Central Fire District of Santa Cruz County, told Outside on November 17.

The enormous swells were generated by powerful low-pressure systems over the northeastern Pacific, where hurricane-force winds pushed waves toward the California coast, according to the National Weather Service. On November 14, forecasters predicted breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet, with occasional sets reaching 40 to 50 feet at big-wave surfing spot Mavericks, near Half Moon Bay.

Bauen, who spent about 20 years as a rescue swimmer, said waves are reaching roads, cliffs, and beach access points earlier in the season than usual.

“The ocean is extremely dynamic, and where there used to be a safe amount of space to recreate even on the beach, those spaces are becoming fewer and further between because of the erosion along our coastline,” he said.

On November 14, rescue crews pulled three surfers from the water near Pleasure Point in Santa Cruz County. A fire department rescuer had picked up two surfers on a jet ski when a large wave overturned the watercraft, throwing all three into the ocean.

The rescuer, a part of Bauen’s team, managed to right the jet ski and continue the operation, returning about ten minutes later to help a third surfer.

Hundreds of miles south that same day, a San Diego lifeguard swam through powerful breaking waves to reach a struggling swimmer at La Jolla Cove. Another lifeguard eventually arrived on a jet ski and brought both men to safety.

Also in San Diego on November 14, at nearby Windansea Beach, a teenager photographing the waves from nearby rocks was swept into the ocean. A surfer jumped into the water and briefly helped keep the teenager’s head above the surface before waves carried him toward the rocky shoreline, where several bystanders helped pull him out.

The close call underscored warnings from San Diego Lifeguard Chief Daniel Orloff that even spectators watching from dry land were at risk. “If you are close, at any moment, a wave could take you out. It can breach a bluff, a berm, even the boardwalk,” he told ABC 10News.

In Orange County, a surfer helped rescue three people struggling in strong currents at Crystal Cove State Beach on November 15, according to a witness who shared video of the aftermath with TV station 10 News San Diego.

Not every incident ended in a rescue. On November 14, a man disappeared while swimming near Zuma Beach in Malibu. Lifeguards responded to the scene around 1:40 p.m., and Coast Guard helicopters and boat crews searched for the missing swimmer into the following day. The Coast Guard suspended its search on November 15 without locating him. The man has not publicly been identified.

Bauen said the ocean can also lull people into a false sense of security. During these swells, waves can stay relatively small for 15 or 20 minutes at a time, making conditions look calm before a surge of much larger waves suddenly arrives and catches surfers off guard.

Rising tides can also leave surfers stranded when the beach access points they used to enter the water become submerged.

While the largest waves have eased, forecasters say hazardous surf will linger through November 19. In its November 17 forecast, the National Weather Service predicted breaking waves of 13 to 17 feet along portions of the Bay Area and Central Coast through November 18, with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.

Bauen urged surfers and beachgoers to check the forecast, pay attention to changing conditions, and identify a safe route back to shore before entering the water.

“Ultimately, it comes down to the individual,” Bauen said. “You really need to know before you go. You need to tune into the ocean conditions, look up forecasts, and do a little bit of research before you explore a secluded beach, decide to go for a swim, or paddle out.”

#8263. 6 Forgotten Backpacking Skills Every Hiker Should Master

Here at Backpacker, we respect old-school cool. It’s not that we’re Luddites or avoid new ways of doing things—from lightweight internal-frame backpacks to gourmet freeze-dried meals, there’s no denying that most modern backpacking developments have made our experiences better. But there’s something about seeing a hiking buddy solve a problem with a retro skill that we admire. It shows knowledge, competence, and the kind of self-reliance that every backpacker secretly aspires to.

Calling the following six low-tech, high-technique skills “lost” might be a stretch—they definitely still have their fans, and every Backpacker editor has used them at least a few times. But they aren’t part of the average beginner hiker’s repertoire anymore, and many hikers go their whole careers without using them. Start practicing them now to level up your skills for next season.

Whether they’re tying their tent’s guylines or their shoelaces, too many backpackers reach for the same overhand knot; it mostly works, but it lacks a certain… elegance? While you don’t need a Boy Scout’s skill at knotcraft to go backpacking, learning to use the right knot for each job will help you finish camp setup quickly and break it down without spending ten minutes coaxing apart the granny knot you’ve welded into your cord. Here are a couple to get you started (check out our guide to the 5 Essential Backpacking Knots for videos and in-depth descriptions):

Slippery Backpacker’s Hitch: Good for hanging bear bags or rigging ridgelines for tarps, and comes undone with a pull. Wrap the rope at least three times around a tree or post, then tuck a bight of the loose end under the last loop.

Bowline Knot: A bombproof method for creating a strong loop. Make a loop in the rope; take the loose end and bring it up through the loop, around the rope, and back down through the loop. (You may or may not catch those of us who learned in school muttering “rabbit comes out of the hole, goes around the tree, and goes back in the hole” while we tie it.) Finish with an overhand and a half-hitch.

Sheet Bend: Need to attach two lengths of cord of different diameters? Create a bight with the bigger cord; bring the end of the thinner cord up through, wrap it around the back of the bight, and run it through the loop it creates.

Lightweight, direct-from-manufacturer shelters and quilts mean that there’s little practical reason to sew your own kit nowadays. However, for those who do like to get handy, the proliferation of patterns for sale and online tutorials on places like YouTube means that it’s never been easier to join the MYOG community. Plus, much like growing your own vegetables, sewing a few pieces yourself will give you a new appreciation for the ingenuity and labor that goes into making your gear.

Instead of jumping straight into the deep end with a high-investment piece like a tent or quilt, start small: A “ditty bag” is perfect for holding small items or replacing a torn or lost stuff sack. See our step-by-step instructions from our Spring 1973 issue, which is easy to sew without a machine. All you’ll need is ¾-yard of ripstop nylon, 30 inches of cord, needles, and thread.

Camp baking is everything modern backpacking meals aren’t: messy, ingredient-heavy, and slow. But there’s a kind of magic in coaxing a loaf of bread or a pizza into existence in the middle of the woods. It may not be an efficient way to eat, but it’s a rewarding skill, and as a party trick, guaranteed to impress your backcountry partners.

The most traditional method is to bake in a Dutch oven using campfire. One easier and lighter way to start: Make a cupcake on your camp stove, which is satisfying and near-foolproof. You’ll need a single-wall steel or titanium mug, a pot big enough to fit it inside, and a lid, plate, or aluminum foil to cover it. Empty a packet of microwaveable cake mix into the mug, add three tablespoons of water, and stir. Drop three small rocks into the bottom of your pot, balance the mug on top of them, and add enough water to the pot that it reaches the level of the cake mix. (If the mug starts to float, you’ve added too much.) Cover and simmer for 20 minutes, then enjoy straight out of the mug. Bonus: also works with pancake mix.

Even if most hikers have moved on to screened-in lightweight tents, flat tarps still have dedicated fans. Besides the unbeatably low weight, there’s a simplicity to making a shelter from a rectangle of fabric that we can still appreciate. (Looking for your first? Borah’s Silpoly Solo Tarps are solid, and at less than $90, eminently affordable.)

There are innumerable ways to pitch a tarp, but the simple plow point shelter is a good place to start. Stake out three corners of your tarp, then use one of your trekking poles to raise the fourth, tensioning it with a guyline. (Pro tip: The first time you do this will take some trial and error to get a good pitch, so give yourself extra time in camp.) For extra dirtbag points, use a 9 x 10 scrap of Tyvek instead; create the guy-out points by pinching a bit of the material around a smooth pebble and tying off the base with a cord.

Whittling is one of those camp pastimes that’s largely fallen by the wayside—but to be fair, today’s backpackers are less likely than their predecessors to spend a lot of time kicking around camp. Still, basic knife skills are good to have in your pocket—you never know when you may need to carve a replacement for a snapped stake or shave tinder to build a fire—and whittling is a good, low-stakes way to practice those skills.

Carving a spoon is an easy project (and a useful one, if you forget your own utensil). Split a piece of deadfall, preferably still green. Carve your spoon’s outline, then hollow out the bowl. (You may have an easier time carving a shovel-shaped bowl than a traditional round one with a typical straight pocketknife.)

Once upon a time, planning a route for our magazine meant taking a walk down to the small library of guidebooks and topo maps we kept in the office and poring through them until we found the trail we were looking for. The world has changed since then—today’s mapping tools are quick and reliable for assembling a plan—but sketching out a trip the old-school way is still a good exercise for your brain. Plus, it can help prevent the kind of careless line-following that regularly gets hikers into trouble.

Picking up an expert-written guidebook for an area you plan on visiting regularly is always a good investment. Otherwise, the public library is your friend: Your local branch likely stocks an array of up-to-date guides, or can obtain them for you via interlibrary loan. Instead of carrying the whole thing, xerox the pages you need and jot points of interest and notes right on the copies. Pair with a compass and a current topo map (your library may stock those, too), and don’t forget to check with rangers or local hikers for the latest beta before you set out.
